explanations.answer: He's a head taller than anyone
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Saul, the son of Kish, was "…a head taller than any of the people." That comes right after the text calls him choice and handsome, without equal among the Israelites. I'm a cookie stamper, so a head taller than anyone is a view I'll never know.

explanations.answer: He's the fastest runner in Israel
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text never says Saul could outrun anybody. It says he was "…a head taller than any of the people." Height is the detail the text gives, so that's the one to keep. Speed would've been handy for chasing donkeys, though.

explanations.answer: He's the strongest man in Benjamin
explanations.explanation: Saul's father Kish is called a powerful man, so I see why strength came to mind. But for Saul himself, the text says he was "…a head taller than any of the people." Nothing in it calls him the strongest in Benjamin. Keep an eye on which man gets which description.

Close, but they don't find them there. The text says they went through the land of Benjamin, "…and still they did not find them." That's four regions in a row with nothing to show for it. I bet their sandals were done with this trip.

That's right, baker. Saul and the servant go through the hill country of Ephraim, Shalishah, Shaalim and the land of Benjamin, and "…still they did not find them." Four stops and no donkeys. That's a long walk for a very quiet result.
Not quite. Saul never mentions the dark. He says, "Come, let us go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us." His reason is about his father at home.

Right. Saul's reason has nothing to do with dark. He says, "Come, let us go back, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us." I think that's a son who knows exactly how long he's been gone.

explanations.answer: Tell them which way to go
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The servant says, "Perhaps he will tell us which way to go." They've walked through all those regions without finding the donkeys, so he's hoping the man of God can point the way. Sometimes you just need somebody to say turn left.
I like the creativity, but the servant never asks for donkeys. He says, "Perhaps he will tell us which way to go." They're after directions, not a loaner herd.
That sounds nice, but it isn't what the servant says. He hopes the man of God will tell them which way to go. The hope is about finding their way, and the text doesn't mention a blessing.

Yes, baker. The servant says, "I have here in my hand a quarter shekel of silver." Saul had just pointed out that the bread in their packs was gone and they had no gift. So the servant's pocket change solves the problem.
Not quite. The servant doesn't pull out any spices. He says, "I have here in my hand a quarter shekel of silver." Silver is what he offers to give the man of God.

A gold ring would've been fancy, but the text doesn't have one. The servant offers "…a quarter shekel of silver." It's a small gift, but it answers Saul's worry about having nothing to take the man of God.

That's right. The writer says, "…the prophet of today was formerly called the seer." The word changed over time, but it's the same kind of person. So when Saul and the servant say seer, the writer's readers would say prophet.
Good guess, but priest isn't the word the writer uses. The text says "…the prophet of today was formerly called the seer." Seer and prophet go together here, and priest doesn't.
Good thought, but the writer doesn't use judge. The side note says "…the prophet of today was formerly called the seer." That's the word to keep.

Yes, baker. The young women say, "Yes, he is ahead of you…" and then, "Hurry now." He had come to the city that day because the people had a sacrifice on the high place. Saul and the servant picked the right moment to show up.

explanations.answer: He left this morning for Ramah
explanations.explanation: Not what they say. The young women answer, "Yes, he is ahead of you…" Samuel is still on his way, and they tell Saul and the servant to hurry. Nobody says anything about him leaving.
The text doesn't say that. The young women tell them, "Hurry now, for today he has come to the city…" and that they'll find him before he goes up to the high place. He's close, not away for the day.

Right. The young women say, "The people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice…" After that, the guests eat. So a whole crowd is standing there with empty plates waiting on one man. I know that feeling when a batch is almost out of the oven.
Not quite. The text says, "The people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice; after that, the guests will eat." So the people wait for Samuel. Nobody is digging in early.
That's it. The text says Samuel was "…coming toward them on his way up to the high place." That's where the sacrifice is. Saul and the servant happen to meet him at the city entrance.
The text doesn't send Samuel home here. It says he was "…on his way up to the high place." The sacrifice is waiting there.
Bethel shows up later in this passage, but not as Samuel's destination. Here the text says Samuel was "…on his way up to the high place." That's where the people are waiting for him.

explanations.answer: A man from Benjamin will come
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The LORD tells Samuel, "At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin…" And Saul is a Benjamite, the son of Kish, who was from Benjamin. The LORD had told Samuel the day before Saul ever arrived.

explanations.answer: A man from Ephraim will come
explanations.explanation: Ephraim is a place Saul passes through while searching, but it isn't what the LORD says. He tells Samuel, "At this time tomorrow I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin…" Benjamin is the one to remember.

explanations.answer: A man from Judah will come
explanations.explanation: Not quite. The LORD says, "…I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin…" Judah isn't mentioned. Benjamin is Saul's tribe.

That's the word. The LORD says, "…you are to anoint him ruler over My people Israel…" Saul came looking for donkeys, and the LORD has something else in mind. The man walking up the hill with a servant is about to get a new job.
Close, but priest isn't the word. The LORD says, "…you are to anoint him ruler over My people Israel…" Ruler is the job being given.

Not quite, baker. Prophets do show up later in this passage, so I get the guess. But the LORD tells Samuel to anoint this man "…ruler over My people Israel…" That's the job on the table, and it's a big one for a man who just went out to find donkeys.

Right. The LORD says this man "…will save them from the hand of the Philistines." That's the job laid out for him. And the LORD adds why: "…I have looked upon My people, because their cry has come to Me."
The text doesn't name the Egyptians here. The LORD says, "he will save them from the hand of the Philistines." The Philistines are the ones in this part of the story.
Not what's said. The LORD says the man "…will save them from the hand of the Philistines." That's the enemy named in this passage.

explanations.answer: Eat with him at the high place today
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Samuel says, "Go up before me to the high place, for you shall eat with me today." Saul came to ask about donkeys and gets a seat at the table instead. Not a bad trade.

explanations.answer: Wait at the city gate until evening
explanations.explanation: That's not what Samuel says. He tells Saul, "Go up before me to the high place, for you shall eat with me today." The invitation is to a meal.

explanations.answer: Meet him back here next week
explanations.explanation: Samuel doesn't mention next week. He tells Saul he shall eat with him today, and says, "…when I send you off in the morning, I will tell you all that is in your heart." The invitation is for today's meal.
Not quite. Samuel says the opposite: "…do not worry about them, for they have been found." Saul can stop searching. That's one worry off the list.

That's right. Samuel tells Saul, "As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found." The reason Saul left home is already settled. And Samuel has more to say after that.

explanations.answer: He says his tribe and clan are the smallest
explanations.explanation: That's it. Saul says, "Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin?" Then he asks why Samuel would say such a thing. I think he's trying to tell Samuel he's got the wrong guy.

explanations.answer: He says he isn't old enough to lead anyone
explanations.explanation: Saul never mentions his age. He says, "Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin?" His answer is about his tribe and clan.

explanations.answer: He says his father needs him back at home
explanations.explanation: Saul did worry about his father earlier, but that's not his answer here. He says, "Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin?" He calls his clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin.

You've got it. Samuel "…seated them in the place of honor among those who were invited—about thirty in all." That puts a man who came looking for donkeys in the place of honor. The servant is seated there too.

Not quite. Nobody is told to wait in the corner. The text says Samuel seated them "…in the place of honor…" Saul and his servant came in as guests, seated among those who were invited, about thirty in all.
Not what the text says. Samuel seated Saul and his servant "…in the place of honor among those who were invited…" They're guests, not helpers.

Right. Samuel says, "Here is what was kept back. It was set apart for you." He adds that it "…has been kept for you for this occasion…" That portion had been waiting since Samuel said he had invited the people.

Not quite, baker. Samuel says the portion "…was set apart for you." and "…has been kept for you for this occasion…" He says it was kept for Saul from the time he invited the people. It was put aside before Saul ever sat down.

explanations.answer: So Samuel can reveal the word of God
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Samuel says, "…you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God." So the servant goes on ahead, and the two of them are left alone. Something important is coming.

explanations.answer: So Samuel can pray for his family
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Samuel tells Saul, "…you stay for a while, and I will reveal to you the word of God." That's the reason he gives.

explanations.answer: So Samuel can bless his trip home
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Samuel says he'll reveal "…the word of God." That's the reason Saul stays behind, not a blessing for the trip. Samuel has the servant go on ahead, so the two of them are left alone.

That's right, baker. Samuel "…took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul’s head, kissed him…" That's what anointing looks like here. Then he asks, "Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?"
Not quite, baker. The text says Samuel "…poured it on Saul’s head…" The oil goes on Saul, and that's how he's anointed. Then Samuel asks, "Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?"

explanations.answer: Gives it to Saul to keep
explanations.explanation: Samuel doesn't hand over the flask. He "…poured it on Saul’s head…" It's an anointing, not a gift to carry home. Then he asks, "Has not the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance?"

You've got it. Samuel says the three men "…will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands." The three are carrying goats, bread and wine, and the loaves are what Samuel says they'll give him.
The men are carrying young goats, so I see the mix-up. But Samuel says they'll give Saul "…two loaves of bread…" The goats aren't part of what he says they'll give.
One of the men does carry a skin of wine. But what they give Saul is "…two loaves of bread…" The wine isn't part of the gift.

explanations.answer: The Spirit of the LORD will rush upon him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Samuel says, "Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them…" He says the prophets will be preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres. Saul joins in with something much bigger than an instrument.

explanations.answer: He will be handed a harp and told to play
explanations.explanation: Harps are in the picture, but Samuel never says Saul gets handed one. He says, "…the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them…" The harps come before the prophets, and nothing in the text hands one to Saul.

explanations.answer: He will be chased off by the Philistines
explanations.explanation: The Philistines do have an outpost at Gibeah of God, but Samuel says nothing about a chase. He says the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon Saul. That's what happens next.
Right. Samuel says, "…you will be transformed into a different person." That comes right after he says the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon Saul. Big change for a man who set out to find donkeys.

Not quite. Samuel says, "…you will be transformed into a different person." That's part of what he tells Saul about Gibeah. It comes right after he says the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon Saul and he will prophesy.
Yes, baker. Samuel says, "When these signs have come, do as the occasion demands, for God is with you." That's the reason Saul can move forward. The one with him is God.
Samuel is the one talking, so I get it. But he says, "…for God is with you." It's God's presence that matters.
Kish is Saul's father, and Samuel does say the men will tell Saul that Kish has started worrying about him. But Samuel says, "…for God is with you." That's the one who's with Saul.

explanations.answer: Offer sacrifices and show Saul what to do
explanations.explanation: That's right. Samuel says, "…surely I will come to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings." He also says, "Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do." So Saul is told to wait for instructions.

explanations.answer: Lead the army against the Philistines
explanations.explanation: Not what Samuel says. He tells Saul he will come "…to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings." and show him what to do. No army is mentioned.

explanations.answer: Bring Saul back home to his father
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Samuel says he'll come to Saul at Gilgal to offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings, and "…show you what you are to do." Saul's father isn't part of that plan.
You've got it. The text says, "…God changed Saul’s heart…" It happens as he turns to leave Samuel. Whatever else changed that day, the text starts there.
Saul keeps his name through the whole passage. The text says, "…God changed Saul’s heart…" Heart is the answer.
Not quite, baker. The text says nothing about Saul's face. It says, "…God changed Saul’s heart…" and that happens as he turns to leave Samuel.
Not quite. The text says, "…all the signs came to pass that day." That's one day, not weeks. Samuel's list was long, and it all fit into that one day.
That's right. The text says, "…all the signs came to pass that day." Every one of them, same day. That's a lot of fulfilled words in one stretch of road.

explanations.answer: What has happened to the son of Kish
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The people who knew him asked one another, "What has happened to the son of Kish?" They had watched him prophesy with the prophets. I think they were just trying to make sense of what they saw.

explanations.answer: Who taught the son of Kish to play
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have that question. The people ask one another, "What has happened to the son of Kish?" It's about what has happened to Saul.

explanations.answer: When did the son of Kish come back
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The people who had known Saul ask, "What has happened to the son of Kish?" Nothing in that question is about his return. I think they're surprised by what they see, since they'd just watched him prophesying with the prophets.
Not quite. The text says, "…Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship." He only told him the donkeys had been found. The rest he kept to himself.

That's right. When his uncle asks what Samuel said, Saul says, "He assured us that the donkeys had been found." Then the text says, "But Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship." He kept that part quiet.
